utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Madam Registrar, and good morning, everybody. Could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record, all the accused are here. From the Defence teams, I only notice the absence of Mr. Haynes. The Prosecution, it's Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Thayer. I understand there are some preliminaries that you wish to raise, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: There is indeed a preliminary I would like to do at this time, and it has to do with the next witness, but we believe that the Trial Chamber should be informed at this point. And it is simply that it is an application to delay the cross-examination of this witness, but only until tomorrow morning. And I'd like to explain why this is so. This has to do, Mr. President, with the fact that we have encountered difficulties with the interview which was provided by this witness on the 21st of July of 2006.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. We're talking of PW-108?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: PW-108, the next witness, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I just wanted to make sure, since there was some change in the order in which -- okay, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The situation is as follows: We have received a second revised translation concerning Witness PW-108 on the last week after business hours on Monday, the 27th of August, following which we have been working to try and make up whether the second revised translation was accurate or not. We have found that it was not, and we have communicated with the Prosecution on Sunday afternoon to indicate that there were further changes and that we wanted to work, during the cross-examination of this witness, with a clean copy of the statement or the interview. What I mean by "a clean copy" is that what we've been provided with is where there was mistakes in translation, they've been crossed out, and then there was two slashes added. The correct translation is in italics, followed by two slashes. It makes the interview very difficult to work with and to read, and makes it also difficult to follow if we have to use it during the cross-examination. Now, this is what we indicated to the Prosecution, and that was on Sunday afternoon. On Monday morning, which is yesterday, I provided to my colleagues from the Prosecution first a clean copy, which is having removed the incorrect parts translated and crossed out in the statement, and I provided them with a series of new changes which we believe, after listening over and over again to this interview on tape, were needed to be made. This prompted a meeting between the Prosecution and the Defence yesterday afternoon. This was attended by two persons on behalf -- three persons on behalf of the Defence of Mr. Nikolic, and this meeting lasted from 2.00 in the afternoon until about 4.30 in the afternoon yesterday, agreeing on most changes that should be brought to this interview. What happened then is that we -- despite the fact that we were in constant contact with the Prosecution, we received a third revised translation at 9.30 or 9.22 exactly last night. And at 9.22, looking at this third translation, there are still some difficulties with this translation. The following difficulties are: First of all, it was provided to us, from a technical point of view, in a format which could not be scanned immediately last night, but that's a minor difficulty which has been, since then, sorted out. The second difficulty is that there are a few more changes that we had proposed that had not been agreed to by the Prosecution. We're trying to get those sorted out this morning, and that's not a major difficulty, either. The major difficulty, Mr. President, is that because of the changes, we do not agree on the format in this interview should appear if it is to be used with the witness. The Prosecution insists and we have received some what they call guidance as to how to read the annotations on the interview. We received this last night at, it was sent at 9.25, but we only realised we had received it around 10.00. And I also received a long e-mail by my colleague from the Prosecution explaining his position with respect to the interview. Basically, what they say is that the portions that have been corrected, where the interpretation was incorrect, should remain on the interview transcript and be crossed out, followed, as I've explained, by the two slashes and then the correct version in italics. We believe, Mr. President, that this is not a proper way to use the statement, if it is to be used, because it does make -- it just changes and alters the interview itself and makes it very difficult to understand what the witness actually said and what is really that he said during the interview that can be used during cross-examination. So that's the first part that we still need to agree upon as to how it will appear, if it's going to be used. The other difficulty I personally had was that my cross-examination is quite long for this witness, I have three hours to cross-examine him. All the questions, I did not have enough time, having received the last version last night, to try and incorporate the changes, because every question I have, where I took lines of the transcript of the interview, I have to change the image. Basically, it's to go back into the statement, scan as an image those two or three lines that go with each of my questions, and to insert them back into my questions. And it has not been possible for me to do that at the late time we received the translation yesterday. For all these reasons, I simply suggest, Mr. President, that the Prosecution can proceed with its examination-in-chief today, and we will proceed the first time -- at the beginning of the day tomorrow with the cross-examination. Another detail which I guess my colleague will explain to you from the Beara team is they did not receive that copy of the new -- the third revised translation of this interview. I provided them with -- the Beara team and I was in contact with them last night from about 9.00 when I started dealing with my colleague over the phone, but that's -- I guess he can explain that. And I understand from my colleague that this may cause for him some scheduling problem. We're fully aware of that, and the idea is we just want to be able to proceed on a sound basis for the cross-examination of Witness PW-108. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question, Mr. Bourgon. Which version of the statement has been the subject of these alterations, the English or the B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Both, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Both of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Both of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It was a very -- the Prosecution will concede that it was indeed pretty difficult work on the part of the translator who was present.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. And my second question is: Was the interview tape-recorded, by any chance?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It was indeed, Mr. President. That's what we've been working on is from the tape. The problem is many words on the tape have been attributed to the witness, and these words were not said by him. So now we have kind of an interview where half of a sentence, for example, we have underlined, and beside that it says: "Not mentioned by the witness." Who mentioned it in that interview room, it could be -- I think there was about five persons there, or at least four, and it's not known who said those words. We take the view that only the words of the witness should be on the tape -- on the transcript so that we know what he said. The Prosecution will argue otherwise and they will say whatever is said in the room of the interview should be in the transcript, and we disagree on this aspect of the interview transcript. And of course we believe that -- as you know, Mr. President, the Trial Chamber has seen the interview a long time ago. The final product that we have today is quite different from what the Trial Chamber operated with when there was a series of motions linked to that witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I would have to say that I fully agree with my colleague, Mr. Bourgon. It was, I say, after 10.00 when I received a phone call from him. I checked my web mail. The Prosecution sent me no new version, although they knew -- had to have known that there's only two teams that are interested in cross-examining this witness. He was nice enough, Mr. Bourgon, to send me a copy, which ultimately was printed out probably after 10.30 last night. So now we literally have three versions that we've been working with. They overlap, they're jumbled, and it's quite a chore. I'm frankly still working on it. I was up late last night, early this morning, and I'm still working on it. And I just don't think it's fair, and I believe that it wouldn't inconvenience anybody that much to let us do our cross tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Meek. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone. I'll try to be as brief as I can, because I just frankly don't want to waste further time on this issue. Let me just provide some factual context to what's going on here. The English and B/C/S transcripts in their original form were disclosed to all Defence on 18 May, along with the tapes. Those went over months ago. The interpretation in the field for this interview, we all agree, was poor, and that is what's creating the problems. It's a matter of the interpreter alone, and it is the interpreter's voice alone which is being corrected here in the transcript. So it's not a question, for example, of if there is something crossed out and it's wrong, there's any question that it's somebody else in the room saying it. The problem we have is in some cases the interpreter ad-libbed, freelanced, as it were, and either characterised by himself what he thought the person was saying, instead of doing a straight interpretation, and in some cases just said things that we can't find any basis for in the witness's actual answer. In some cases, the interpretation was factually incorrect, and those have been corrected as well. The reason why we insist that these corrections be made plain is that that most faithfully reflects what actually was said and heard during the course of the interview. We have a very simple legend or guide which we've provided. It's identical to the guide that was provided with respect to the interview of Mr. Borovcanin. It is helpful to all parties so that you can hear what is exactly being said, whether it is right or wrong. It is imperative that everybody be able to follow that if you're actually listening to the tape in realtime and want to exactly know what, factually, was being said during the course of the interview. I understand that my colleague wants to provide some kind of a clean -- so-called clean version that only has the very words that the witness, himself, said so that there's sort of an uninterrupted answer, but that doesn't really reflect the reality of what was going on in that interview, for better or worse, and unfortunately we all agree that it was a rough interview because of the interpretation. This witness is an intelligent person. We are confident that with some elementary explanation of how to follow the changes that we've made, the sort of editorial symbols, that it will not be difficult for him to follow along if he is ever refreshed or confronted with a transcript of his interview. What we have simply done is if there was a word that was incorrectly interpreted or a phrase incorrectly interpreted, we've drawn a line through it, and then right next to that in italics we have inserted what we all agree is the correct word or phrase. If the witness simply didn't say what is represented to be in the transcript by the interpreter, we again indicate that that is the case: "Not said by witness." If there was an instance where something wasn't translated to the witness or interpreted to the witness by the interpreter, we have indicated that, too, by an abbreviation. It's very simple, everybody can follow along. Without that, however, one has no sense of what actually was going on in this interview, and again it is not the case that there is something, for example, that the investigator jumped in, in the middle of an answer, and was misattributed, as far as I know, to the witness. It is really simply a matter of trying to make heads and tails out of what the interpreter said. Now, as I understand it, what we have remaining are four words or phrases that, after last night's exercise, my friends have brought to our attention that weren't changed in the revision. Let me make it clear: When my friends approached us yesterday with numerous suggested changes, we sat down with them, worked with them for two hours, and made those changes, all of them. We did not dispute a single change, as far as I know, that they made. As I understand it, there are four changes that weren't made, but I don't believe that that is a matter of us disagreeing. I think it was most likely just something that got missed last night as it was being done in the evening. I will have an update in a few moments, but it is simply four words or phrases that are still outstanding. I think we've remained very flexible throughout -- throughout, and with respect to this witness, who was originally scheduled to testify in mid-June, we have had a series of continuances at the Defence request, none of which we've opposed, all of which we have -- thought were appropriate. We have worked very hard with them to furnish any and all information that they have requested, and they have suggested a tremendous amount of additional information that we have gone ahead and furnished. So what I don't understand is why, at this late stage, we are being told that these changes, which are changes suggested by the Defence and which we have made, they cannot proceed at all with the cross-examination. Now, as for my friends on the Beara team, you know, I've got a phone, everybody knows all my phones and my e-mails. Certainly the Nikolic team does, so I can't speak to why I wasn't contacted about this. We have been working with this team to address their concerns. I was not aware that any other team had any specific concerns at all. We are ready to go with this witness. We agreed to change the witness order this week, I thought, so that they would be prepared to deal with some new materials that they had requested from some commission somewhere, and now we are being -- we are being told that they are unable to proceed at all because there's a problem with the transcript. Again, we have a scheduling issue with respect to the videolink which is set in stone because of the location which it is being done. We anticipate that will take at least Wednesday and probably part of Thursday. We have asked the people on site to be prepared to sit Thursday as well. We have another witness scheduled who is coming from abroad to begin testimony, Witness 101, on Thursday, and we have Witness 119 who has his own logistical situation that has to be addressed by the DU to bring him in on Friday. That, I'm less concerned about because we can have him postponed, but it will create, I think, some problems in terms of scheduling. We have already adjusted the schedule this week. This witness is ready to go. He's been here since Sunday. I don't see why we can't begin cross-examination on some topic. They've estimated three hours of cross-examination, and we're ready to proceed. Again, I don't think any of these issues are issues that we can't resolve this morning, and we're resolving them right now, as I understand it, so we should have an agreed transcript to work with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Mr. Meek, and then you, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Thayer is missing the point completely. We're not saying that -- at least I'm not saying that we can absolutely not continue with the cross-examination or do it. The fact is that this is a Prosecution witness. This is a tape-recording done by the Prosecution. It's their witness. They have the burden of proof. They should have had this cleaned up a long time ago. The clean version is not really the issue. They say the witness, he's intelligent, he can follow along, but there again we have, I believe, the right to adequately represent our clients. Our clients have to have effective assistance of counsel, and to do that -- the client may be able to follow along, but if a lawyer for the accused has these things dumped on him at the 11th hour, then it's just not fair. Mr. Thayer says, "Well, I don't know, everybody's got my phone number." I don't have his cell phone at 10.30 at night, number one. And, number two, I don't know that it's my burden to have to call every night and say, "Did you send anything new to any other accused team that you didn't send to me?" The obligation of the Prosecutor is to send --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: -- anything to everybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. Thank you. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I don't dispute the fact that we received the statement on 18 May. I think that's not really the point here, Mr. President. I believe that there has been some good work accomplished on both sides of this courtroom in dealing with this interview. It's been a very, very difficult task to perform the changes, which have led to the second revision that we received last week. Now, there are two issues here, Mr. President. The first one is the changes that appear on the transcript of the interview, and then the short delay that we request in order to be ready to prepare. Now, let me just use one example of what is in the interview transcript to say why we insist that it be a clean copy. At one point, the witness is asked, and I quote now from the version I have, which is the latest third revised translation, page 9 of 20. The question at line 16 is: "You could -- you could see the buses?" And then there is something called "TTRV" and slash, which I believe means not correctly interpreted from the B/C/S. And then it says: "Buses and trucks." Then the answer at line 17 is: "Yes." And then this is changed between slash: "Yes, from here" slash. Then it says: "I could see the buses and trucks there on that main road there," followed by a slash: "Not said by RV." Slash: "But I didn't know --" this is crossed out and replaced in slash by: "It wasn't known where they were going and who was inside." From this paragraph, if we give it to the witness, it can, for one, suggest a different answer, it can be -- make it more difficult, and it would be much more appropriate simply to operate with what is exactly said on the tape, without any additions or subtractions or things that are crossed out. I think this would make it much easier, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, thank you. Yes, Mr. Thayer, do you wish to add anything, and that will be the end of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Yes, just two brief things. (redacted) (redated)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: -- of so -- and again my friend just said it would be much more appropriate simply to operate with what is exactly said on the tape. That is exactly our point. If you want to know what was said on the tape, you need, unfortunately, to have a key such as this so you can follow what was said on the tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, so that we get a clear picture, how long do you expect your examination-in-chief of PW-108 to last?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: I think about 45 minutes to an hour, tops, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And then we have -- between the Beara and the Nikolic team, we already have four hours, 15 minutes, four hours, 15 minutes. We have approximately -- we have lost half an hour already. We have another 30 minutes, at least, with Simanic. That's one hour and a half. Let's -- The most important thing, because trying to condense all the debate, I think from what I have heard, you are in a position to come out with a version of the interview, both in English and in B/C/S, which reflects the entirety of what you have agreed upon. Now, whether that should be then annotated or not, or whether the annotations should be made use of -- one moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think, in a way, without trying to diminish in any way the importance of your submissions, which are extremely relevant and we needed to know this, of course, before we proceeded any further, I think one could condense it as follows: There should be what you both consider to be the correct transcript of the interview of this person, particularly in relation to the witness, I would be referring to the B/C/S version because that's what he will be shown if he is shown the transcript of his statement or not. In relation to the English version -- in relation to the English version, I think it is important that there is a clean -- what Mr. Bourgon referred to as a clean copy, basically reflecting the transcript of the interview that you have agreed upon, but the annotations are also very important. I mean, they need not be shown to the witness, but they are important.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Look, our position is as follows, having heard your submissions: Let me verify one thing first with you to make sure that I gave the right information to my colleagues. During the interview, was the procedure as follows: An investigator from the OTP puts a question in English, it is interpreted to the witness in Serbo-Croat, the witness answers in Serbo-Croat, it is interpreted into English, and the statement or the purported statement of the witness is drawn up in English. Then it is translated later on into B/C/S. As soon -- when I say "later on," as soon as it is -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The procedure, Mr. President, is: When we bring the tape back from the interview, it is -- a transcript is made by a B/C/S language assistant who generates a version in B/C/S, and then an English --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But, Mr. Thayer, at the end of the interview, wasn't a document already existing?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. In these interviews there's -- you mean a witness statement of some kind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. It's just a straight question-and-answer interview, and the only thing that's left at the end of this interview is a tape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: So there's no actual witness statement of any kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, that reinforces the rationale behind the decision that we are going to give; namely: As I said, there must be and there should be available for the witness, if he is referred to his statement, a clean copy of his purported statement to the Office of the Prosecutor in the B/C/S language, which, by "clean copy," means a statement which incorporates all the corrections that you have agreed upon. That's number one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In B/C/S, yes, in B/C/S. Then we will need, because of the submissions and the complications that have been mentioned, then we will need, in both languages, in both languages, a statement of the -- not a statement, a transcript of the interview, in which all the alleged or challenged or accepted or unaccepted contentions, relating to correct or incorrect interpretation, need to be indicated. That's the only way we can follow what happened and to what extent there was this wrong interpretation. In other words, the English version would reflect all the changes made and all the alleged wrong interpretations and all the alleged contentions. Similarly, the B/C/S version would reflect the same. We are not saying that these are going to go into the record as exhibits, for the time being, unless there is a specific request, obviously which I don't anticipate, but for an intelligent way of following the evidence or testimony of this person, we need those to have in place. The second thing is the cross-examination. I think let's finish with Mr. Simanic first. Then we start with PW-108 on direct. We'll see where we are after you've finished the examination-in-chief, and then we start with cross-examination on what is possible today. There would be little time available, in any case, but we will start, and then of course you will continue tomorrow. Basically, the bulk will be tomorrow, in any case. Now, there is another thing that we need to decide today, and that relates to a Prosecution motion for protective measures for Witness 88. This is the person whose testimony we are going to receive via videolink. There is a request to have practically the usual -- all the facial, voice distortion and the use of a pseudonym. I would like first to know whether there is any objection on the part of the Defence teams. And, secondly, I would like to make clear one thing: That since this is a videolink, there is no way that technically we can provide for facial distortion and sound distortion during the videolink connection itself. In other words, the testimony of this person will arrive into the courtroom irrespective of whether we put the -- now, I'm not assuming that we are going to give the protective measures. But assuming that we do, his testimony would come here without any facial or sound distortion. In other words, everyone will be able to see him in the face, which begs two questions. The public, and that I think we have more or less agreed already how to go about it, and we will inform you later on; and, secondly, is: How can we make a voice and image distortion effective if it's not being received as such? So what we would do, if we put in place these, is that the broadcast only of the testimony of Witness 88 would be subject to facial and sound distortion. That is possible. I'm informed that technically that is possible. But inside the courtroom, that would not be possible. All right? I don't know if I've made -- I may have complicated it a little too much, but is it clear enough? Okay. So we hear no objections, so the protective measures you have asked for are being granted, with this caveat: That the facial and sound distortion will be applicable only, because of technical restrictions, in relation to the outside broadcast of the proceedings and this Trial Chamber. And then we will tell you later on how to proceed in case we have members of -- persons in the public gallery, how to proceed about that. Okay, thank you. So, Madam Usher, could you kindly bring in the witness, please. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I'd just like to indicate an error in yesterday's transcript. It is on the page 56, line 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I have to bring it up. That's yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In inverted commas, there is just a letter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I won't be able to --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What page?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: 56, line 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now it's already in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is it line starting with: "Absolutely"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. It is my question, and the line started with the word "A" in inverted commas.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: There is just the letter "A" instead the word "and" in inverted commas. That's all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Simanic, good morning to you. Welcome back.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to proceed with your testimony today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Simanic, if we can just proceed. We started the cross-examination briefly yesterday. Good morning to you, sir. Sir, yesterday I asked you if you remember that the Prosecutor told you - and for the Prosecutor's reference, page 25, line 43. Do you remember him telling you, and it was awkwardly written in the transcript, as I probably said it that way that, quote, and this is from the Prosecutor, quote: "I don't think the 5th Engineers killed these people." Do you remember him telling you that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the Prosecutor who was interviewing you in January of 2006 was the gentleman here to your right, correct, the lead senior trial attorney; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, at any time -- strike that. You were present with an attorney at this interview; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At any time, did you or your attorney ask the Prosecutor why you were still a suspect if he told you, as he did on line 33, that he didn't have any indication that the 5th Engineering Battalion murdered anybody at the Kravica warehouse, and subsequently on the same page, line 43, stated that he didn't think that the 5th Engineers killed these people? Did you ever ask him why you were still a suspect then, if he had that opinion in 2006?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did he ever offer an explanation to you as to why you were still a suspect, given what he told you?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He only said that there were some other matters at hand and that this status would continue until those things changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And did he share with you first on the record what those other matters were, or was this a discussion that you had with him off the record?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was when I was being prepared for my testimony on Sunday, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Oh, so you're talking about this past Sunday; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, share them with us, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not able to quote him exactly. He said that this would continue until things changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did he give you an indication of what things would need to change so that this wouldn't continue, that you would be identified as a suspect?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I'd like to talk about, briefly, with respect to the exhibit that we used yesterday, and I think it's P02672, so we'll have that up on the screen for you to see as well. But while that's being brought up on the screen, sir: Yesterday you mentioned that there was antagonism between the police MUP and the army. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And, sir, would you describe that antagonism as being in existence in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe so, I believe it existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you remember, sir, that in your statement, you said that it existed, did you not? And, again, that's on page 59, lines 2 through 8.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have this before me. That's why I'm not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay, fair enough. I'm asking him if he just remembered, Your Honour. We'll show him the document in a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, Mr. Witness, that you also qualified that antagonism and identified it as being strong antagonism between the army and the MUP; do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said there was antagonism between the army and the MUP because the MUP men were better equipped, they had better uniforms, whereas the army did not have such good equipment, and this was the major cause of this antagonism between the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I remember that, thank you. And also do you remember saying that the army and the MUP police were never together and never worked together; do you remember saying that in January of 2006? Page 46, Counsel.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember -- I would only rarely see them working together or working alongside each other on certain tasks. This is what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this, sir: Do you remember, in 1995, a person by the name of Tomo Kovac?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only heard of him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, do you remember what his position was on or about July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that he worked in the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you know what his title specifically was at that time?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not really, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can look at this document that we have before us, P02672, and I understand, quite respectfully, some of your testimony with respect to this document, but I'd like to focus on the part where you discuss the MUP police company, if we may. And perhaps if the Prosecution would be kind enough to give the witness the original, maybe it would help him follow quickly. And that would be under section 2, Your Honours, subsection (f), as it's identified. And, Mr. Witness -- or Mr. Simanic, please tell me when you've had an opportunity to look at that paragraph that's 2(f).

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in the first sentence, it says: "MUP police company: Executing tasks as ordered by its command." I'd like to just focus on that phrase. It does continue on in the sentence, but for my purposes I'd like to focus on that. Am I correct, sir, reading this, and given your testimony about who may or may not have signed this document, "as ordered by its command," is it referring to the police command that was giving orders to these MUP police company personnel?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most probably, because we did not have any influence on them, nor did we know what the police company was involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And when you say you, you're talking about the army, or the 5th Engineering Battalion, or the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the 5th Engineering Battalion, because I don't know much about anybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I'd like to -- and there was a phrase used here, "to give the Court the best possible view of what the truth may be," yesterday on page 41, lines 18 through 19, Counsel. Am I correct, sir, that this strong antagonism that you referenced and that the orders that were given by the Command of the MUP to its police officers is something that occurred either throughout the 1992-1995 period or is it just confined, in your view, to July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's fair, and I'll restate the question. Sir, am I correct that this strong antagonism that you identified, as well as what's written on this document, P02672 on the 14th of July, 1995, that the Command of the MUP that was referenced in this document related to the period of solely July 1995, that the MUP personnel followed the orders of its Command, or was it for a period before that as well, in your view?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already replied about the antagonism. As for obeying commands, I meant the period when they were in Konjevic Polje, because before that we did not know what they were up to, what they were doing, what was their strength, or anything regarding the police.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Sir, I want to also show you the two -- if I -- with the Court's permission, of course, because I want to and it's another phrase that was used by my learned friend, although he just left, that most faithful reflects what you actually said during your interview. And I'd like to, if I may, use the ELMO to show, because there was a discussion as to whether, during your direct examination, whether you said, "Even worse, I signed it," when my learned friend asked you about this document that you have before you. So I'd like to show you the B/C/S version as well as the English version just so that we could compare the two, of course, with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why do you want to show him the English version if yesterday he said he doesn't understand English?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Really for the Court's convenience and for all of us to follow along side by side, Your Honour. I'm not asking him to read the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We can follow. We do have the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour, but I'll just ask him -- and I've highlighted it, but I would ask the usher to show it to my learned friend. And we'll be looking at the English version, Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That needs to be brought up on the screen. It's not in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Page 22, and specifically line 44 on the English version, and we'll see right now that it's, I think, the same page 22 of the B/C/S version, but the line is 22 and 23, if you will. If I may proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Witness, you don't have the English version before you, but looking at the English version, there seems to be some breaks in the text from that which is reflected in the Serbian version, or the B/C/S version, excuse me. And if we look at your line here, 22 and 23, it would seem to be the translated line in English of line 44, with your initials and then a slash for the interpreter, and it says on line 44 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry, but do we have an English version?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I do, but I thought, and I may have misunderstood, that the Court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought it was going to be available on the system, but since it doesn't have a 65 ter number, I think we need to put it -- I think the original now, the B/C/S one, can be handed to the witness, he can keep it in front of him, and we can put on the ELMO the English version now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I think, though, and it's quite candidly a very short exercise, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think if both are just placed on the ELMO, I think we can all see it rather quickly, but I'll do it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, okay, let's proceed in that way, then.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And just for the record, the English version has a pen mark on the right side of the text, and if the usher would be kind enough to show that to the Prosecutor as well. Yes, that page. It's just marked so that we could find direction on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think -- now, Madam, I think if you put one on top of the other so that we can see both highlighted texts, it will be better. Yes, but it has to be brought down now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that would be good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you for your patience, Mr. Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, the reason we insist that these corrections be made plain is that we want most faithfully for it to reflect what was actually said and heard during the course of this interview, and said by my learned friend this morning, in fact. And what I'd like to ask you is that the -- although you don't speak English, the English version reads, and I'll read it for you, on line 44, it says: "And furthermore, even worse, I signed it." Now, would you be kind enough, although that's only seven words, could you read to me what seems to be that which is reflected on lines 22 and 23 of the B/C/S version, again page 22 of that transcript? Can you read that in for the Court, please, so they could follow it as it's translated here verbatim?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I supposed to do that?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "1.000 to 1.500 enemy civilians and soldiers were arrested, killed, and what's even worse, I signed, didn't I?"

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, was that a question that you were asking the Prosecutor as he was making that allegation to you, when you said "didn't I?"

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was my comment, and I said this because at first, like I stated yesterday, at first I thought that it was done by a unit of the 5th Engineers Battalion. That's how it looked to me at first glance. The second part was more like a question both to myself and to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, and I apologise for having to ask you this, but if you look even further above both the English compared to the B/C/S, there seems to be either longer texts in the English version and shorter in the B/C/S, and in some occasions vice versa. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In this specific case --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, because I was trying to understand your question when Judge Kwon commented that he, too, doesn't really understand it. What do you mean exactly, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think if you just look at this page, Your Honour, you'll see it doesn't flow from the B/C/S version precisely compared to the English version. The paragraphs before that are not only lengthier but there's more questions, there's no interruptions. The English version seems to be a somewhat modified version or a summary version, if you will, of what was transcribed in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The criticism or analysis of this should be something that takes place outside of the witness, especially when there's questions along this line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In any case, isn't it there for us to see, Mr. Ostojic, and to attach to it the importance that it deserves?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Most definitely, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's proceed with your next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, you spoke about the Command of the police. Can you describe the Command of the police? Can you describe their structure at all?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know, sir, in this P02672, in the section 2(f) that we were referencing and in the three sections above that, when they said that they would send patrols and organise ambushes, do you know how many patrols were sent and how many ambushes were organised?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where does it say "patrols"?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Paragraph number 2, sir, subsection (b).

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It doesn't say "patrols" anywhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let's look at subsection (b), and if I misspoke, sir, I'll find the specific reference to it. If you look at section (b), sir, I'm focusing on: "Organising ambushes ..." Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know how many ambushes were organised on or before July 14th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What is meant by "ambushes" at guards' posts, because they were trying to reinforce their guards' posts by redeploying the men and by rearranging their numbers, and a special emphasis is put on the guards' posts number 5 and 6. That's why it is phrased as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The gentleman whose initials appear on the back of this page you gave us, his name is Zajo, and Mirko is his first name. What was his -- do you remember his position with the 5th Engineering Battalion in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in charge of -- in charge of all the administration. He was the only one who knew how to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But what was his title, if you remember, specifically?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you remember his rank in July of 1995, what his rank was?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We called him "Zajo" because he was warrant officer second class, hence the nickname "Zajo."

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you, sir, ever go to the Kravica warehouse after July 13th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know if anyone from your 5th Engineering Battalion went to the Kravica warehouse on July 13th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody went there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: One last question. Did my learned friend tell you that your status as a suspect would be changed after you testify or did he give you any indication of when that status would change conveniently?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Ms. Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And if I may just have my transcripts back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. My name is Jelena Nikolic, and I am Defence counsel for Mr. Drago Nikolic. I'd like to ask you a number of questions linked to the document that we've just discussed with my learned friend. Listening to your testimony yesterday and checking out certain information in the transcript of your interview given to the Prosecution, if I understood it correctly, document P02672, or rather it is the order of the 14th -- or combat report, rather, of the 14th of April, 1995, in point 1 it contains a piece of information, and you weren't sure where it came from. It says the 14th of April in the transcript, whereas it's the 14th of July, 1995. Do you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you repeat it, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: The information contained in point 1, and the subtitle, which is "The Enemy," which is contained in the combat report, on the basis of your testimony about that, I understood it that you did not know where it came from and how it came to be contained in this report.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: You had, in your absence, I mean your 5th Engineers Battalion, you had a commander and deputy commander who was on duty, he was an officer on duty?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the barracks, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: We're talking about Konjevic Polje, are we not?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: I assume that he was linked in a system of communications?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He should have been. However, our communications did not function at that time, not a single one.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: So on that 13th and 14th of July, the connections of -- communications of the 5th Engineers Battalion was severed?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think they were severed for a longer time.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: That means that your 5th Engineering Battalion in Konjevic Polje, for that period of time, did not receive any official information from the ground via the communications system?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: Can we agree, sir, that the information contained in point 1, under the heading "Enemy," not to read it once again, and it is this same document number, was based on stories told by people coming into Konjevic Polje, and they conveyed information that hadn't been checked from the ground?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From soldiers coming back from leave, that's where we got the information from, and they were not verified, nor were they checked out.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: And you consider it to be a great mistake on your part that some information that wasn't checked out, you introduced into the report to your unit?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was my mistake, too, but it was also the mistake of the person who received this piece of information for not checking it out.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have no further questions. Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Nikolic. I have next on my list Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I am Defence counsel for Ljubomir Borovcanin. Together with my colleagues, we represent his Defence team, and I have just a few questions to ask you. At one point in time yesterday, you said that you received information to the effect that the Command of the 5th Engineering Battalion was given some days off in June 1995. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me when I say that according to the documents that we have, it was the period from the 9th of July until the 20th of July?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember when I learned about this exactly and how long the period went on for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to clear the record, there was -- it looks like there's been a little translation error. I think you're talking about getting time off in July, not June.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. And I think you would agree to that, Mr. Simanic and Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, Mr. Simanic, that we were talking about July, July 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You did not carry out any official hand-over of duty when the commander of the 5th Engineering Battalion left?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't even say goodbye. I didn't even see him when he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Nobody told you what your duties were, if you were taking over the post of the commander of the 5th Engineering Battalion; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't take over the post of the commander. I was still the deputy commander, if there was no hand-over and takeover of duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We agree, then, that there was no official hand-over of duty?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not official or any other.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, the next thing I wanted to ask you is this: It refers to part of your testimony yesterday, where you mentioned the Konjevic Polje police check-point which was near your guard post, guard post number 6. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Will you tell me when that post was set up?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I think it was in 1990 -- well, it was there when we arrived in Konjevic Polje. It arrived -- it was there before we arrived in Konjevic Polje, the check-point.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, on page 35, line 7, it says "before 1990."

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I stopped. I didn't finish the year. I stopped by saying "1990" and didn't add the year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And which was the year, then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was about to give you the year the check-point was set up, and then I remembered that it was already there when we arrived in Konjevic Polje. So it means that before we arrived, the check-point was already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying it was before 1994?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, because that's roughly when we arrived in Konjevic Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying as well that they were members of the MUP, wearing blue police uniforms; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would I be right in saying, again, that the region of Konjevic Polje belongs to the Zvornik centre?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I do believe that it did belong to them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the presence of a company of special police units of the centre for public security of Zvornik in that area in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey. Wait before you answer the question, please. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think you're talking about PJP units, and there's going to be a big confusion because the word "special" was used in the interpretation. And I'm sure that's not what Mr. -- I'm fairly sure that's what Mr. Stojanovic meant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know what Mr. Stojanovic said because -- I know what we have in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: He used the word that gets always translated as "special," but he did not mean "special." We're back to that situation again. He was not asking about his client's troops at this question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. If you know the correct name, then you can use the correct name straightaway, Mr. Stojanovic, and that would --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's one of the fallacies that's being argued here today is that there's some sort of correct version always. He did use the correct name, but if he would use the initials, I think there might not be a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then perhaps you can, if you agree to that, Mr. Stojanovic, you could use the initials "PJP" or whatever they are.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission, I'd like to thank Mr. McCloskey, but I think we can continue, and I'll say that I will use the initials "PJP" by which we wish to differentiate from the special police brigade, and I think that we have succeeded in doing that so far. So, yes, I will use the "PJP," but the first question was for the benefit of my -- of the witness, because we speak the same language, so we know what we mean. But, anyway, thank you for your assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, just to go back to my question: Do you know that in the region of Konjevic Polje in July, the month of July in 1995, there was one company, the PJP of the Centre for Public Security of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the police rotated. Some would come and others would go. We weren't informed which police unit was there, how many policemen were there and who was actually there, who arrived and who left. So as far as we were concerned, all policemen were the same to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say "the same," do you mean that they were all wearing blue uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, blue uniforms, that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'd like now to use a document, or try to, but I see that we're coming up to the break time. So perhaps I could do that after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you for having noticed that, Mr. Stojanovic. We'll have a 25-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we take a look at Prosecution Exhibit P00006 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we're going to take a look at the document together. May we agree that it is an order by the president of the Republic, Radovan Karadzic, dated the 21st of March, 1995? Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In point 1 of this order, it says the following: "Regarding the relocation of the VRS unit based in Konjevic Polje, immediately take the necessary measures to establish a system of security and control over the uninhabited parts of the territory," mentioned there, as well as two of the roads mentioned here. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in point 2, it says: "Considering the extreme importance of these roads, examine the possibility of stationing some of the MUP units in Konjevic Polje." Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, I assume that you've never seen this document before.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm looking at it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that it says in the heading that the document, or, rather, the order of the 21st of March, 1995, that it is an order of the 21st of March, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Now let us look at another document together. It's a Prosecution exhibit, P00007. Do you have the document in front of you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that at the top of the document, it says it was issued by the Cabinet of the Minister of the Interior on the 23rd of March, 1993 -- 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: May we agree that it was sent to the President of Republika Srpska by the then Minister of the Interior; is that right? That was Zivko Rakic?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And it says that in the area mentioned there, the 2nd Company of the PJP was dispatched of the Zvornik Public Security Centre. Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I assume that you've never seen this document either.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never before. This is the first time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My question to you is as follows: From March 1995, did you know at any time that in this area a company, a PJP company, was deployed of the Zvornik Public Security Centre; did you have an awareness or knowledge of that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I told you a moment ago and I can tell you again that I don't know which one or what the composition was, what the company was, how many men there were, and in the combat report, as a stereotype, they repeat one and the same thing, that is to say, that a police company was deployed there, that it had a check-point, and that it was functioning pursuant to orders from its Command. That's all I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now let me just ask you this in passing: Would you agree with me that there was a check-point there, that the police was there, even after the 20th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard or do you know a man by the name of Mane Djuric who at that time, that is to say in July 1995, performed the function of deputy chief of the JB in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know Mane Djuric from Jasanica. I don't know which post he occupied at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: May we agree that this man, Mane Djuric, whom you say you know and who lived in Jasanica, you say you know he worked in Zvornik, but didn't know which function he had?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he worked in Zvornik during that period, but I don't know what post he occupied or what function he had.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me briefly; just because there's -- as we know, there's more than one Mane Djuric. Are they saying Jasanica or Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You've read my mind, actually, because I was going to put the same question. I thought I heard the witness say Jasanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes. And just to also -- well, I think counsel will clear it up, but just to prevent further confusion, as you know, there's a Mane Djuric of the special police and there's a Mane Djuric of the CJB Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think these are points that are -- that deserve some clarification, Mr. Stojanovic, and I would start first with the town from where this Mane Djuric that you referred the witness to came from. You could ask him to spell the name. I think he's following what I am saying. Mr. Simanic, this Mane Djuric that you knew, where did he come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know where he was born. Before the war, he resided in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Vlasenica. Okay, that's clear enough. And do you know which unit he formed a part of?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a member of the police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Back to you, Mr. Stojanovic, if you can clarify that further.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Since we have two men by the same name working for the MUP, I would like to clarify this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The Mane Djuric that you're talking about that you know, who resided in Vlasenica, worked in the police in Zvornik; am I right in saying that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that at the time, he did work in Zvornik, and after the war I'm sure that he worked in the Zvornik police.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I believe that there are no more doubts about that, and I'm asking you this for the following reason: Do you personally know that at any point in time in July 1995, any kind or sort of order to the PJP company or the police in Konjevic Polje, through you, was sent to anybody?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, this didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The following thing I would like to ask you is this: You looked at the combat report sent on the 14th of July, and you said that you did not know when that was sent to the Drina Corps. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And as you said today, you can't tell us, with any degree of certainty, at what time on the 14th of July was this combat report couriered to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't tell you. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I tell you that we have not got any reports by the 5th Engineers Battalion for the 13th of July and we have one for the 12th and for all the subsequent days, my question is this: Is it possible that you -- not you, personally, but the 5th Engineers Battalion, on the 13th of July, did not send a combat report to the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This should not have taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: If there's none and if something like that should have happened, would then the 14 July report also encompass and include all the events that took place on the day when the report was sent and for the previous day, when the report wasn't sent?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already told you that I don't know. I don't know much about the military administration, and I really can't tell you whether this would have been the case or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, we can agree that you simply don't know what is the time of the events that were contained in the report drafted and sent on the 14th of July; in other words, you don't know whether the events took place on the 13th or on the 14th or on both dates, you simply don't know because you didn't do that?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right, I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. Your Honours, we have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. That leaves Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Mr. Simanic, I'm asking questions on behalf of General Gvero, and it's right, because you've told us already, that you didn't witness any of the fighting on the 13th of July in the Konjevic Polje area between the VRS and the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the wounding of the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, I was going to deal with that specifically in a moment, but I was going to ask you more generally whether you viewed any of the military activity that took place on that day in that place.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that day, I could not see anything because at the time before the noon I wasn't there, and for that reason I was not in a position to observe anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And you've told the Trial Chamber that information about the fighting was brought to your attention by troops returning for home leave; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, that was the only information.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And then in due course, you learnt that two members of your platoon were injured, Mr. Bandjur and Mr. Orasanin; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Did you speak to them subsequently about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who took the record of -- on the wounding spoke to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And we know that they ended up being treated in the medical centre in Zvornik; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know about that. I don't know if both of them ended up being treated in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Could we have a look at P0119, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I don't think you've been shown this document in the course of your testimony over the last couple of days. We can see here a report dated the 13th of July of 1995 to the Command of your battalion, purportedly signed by yourself. It mentions that these two men were wounded at around 8.00 in the morning. And at the very end of the document, it says that Orasanin was treated in the medical centre in Zvornik. And in the sentence immediately above that, it says that Bandjur was as well.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Does that jog your memory as to the fact that these two men required medical treatment in the hospital in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, judging by this document, they did.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And did you speak to them sometime later, maybe a month, maybe two months later, but did you get a chance to speak to these two men about what had happened?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't speak to any of the two of them after their wounding, because after this, they were on sick leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: But it's right that at least other people told you that there had been a firefight that morning in Konjevic Polje; correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I returned to Konjevic Polje, I learnt about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: And the men of the ABiH were armed with fire-arms, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How else would they -- the two soldiers have been wounded?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Precisely. This wasn't a situation where the ABiH were armed with a weapon like a shillelagh; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says here that they were wounded by a pistol, which is certainly not a shillelagh.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Yes. And the fact that this firefight had taken place was confirmed to you? That's really what I want you to confirm, please.

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Josse. I just want to confirm that the Miletic and Pandurevic teams do not wish to cross-examine the witness. All right. Do you have a re-examination, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just very briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sir, do you know a member of the 2nd Company of the PJP Zvornik named Nenad Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And I'd like to show you again the 14 July document and the document mentioned by counsel, a 12 July combat report from your unit as well, and just ask you one or two questions about these, if I could. The 14 July document we know as 2672, and the 12 July document, I guess we'll come up with another number for, but it's ERN 0439-2936. If I could get a little help. Now, I'm not so interested in the content, but could you turn over the 14 July document and look where your signature is? That's, I don't know, about a third of the way down the page. And the 12 -- excuse me, the -- I think that may be wrong. The 12th is a third of the way down the page and the 14th is closer to the bottom. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If you were just taking blank forms or blank reports and signing them, how do you know where to sign the piece of paper on the page?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't say that I only signed blank documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't want to be too involved in this, but I think the translation was not correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think he said, "I didn't say I always signed blank documents," but we could ask him again, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not the same thing, but that's not what he said yesterday, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We might have had a translation glitch. This is a very tough job, being a translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So let's -- I'll just ask you the question again. Can you explain how you would know where to sign these things if you were just signing blank pages, as you had told us before?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When a report had to be drafted, you knew approximately how long the text was going to be, and that's how we did it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Are you now aware of the historical fact that over a thousand Muslims were murdered on 13 July and buried nearby?

utterances.speaker: MILE SIMANIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say if I'm aware?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe that this is beyond the scope of the cross-examination. Nothing to this effect was put to the witness during the cross-examination. A question of this type was never put to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Nikolic. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The questions concerned his knowledge at and around the time of it. I'm just going a little bit further to clarify his knowledge and, therefore, perhaps his credibility on a very related issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
